Generalising odd/even to N threads needs the non-obvious parts: a modulo turn predicate, notifyAll not notify, and a termination rule that does not leave threads parked forever.

The staff/principal favourite: workers blocking on a queue, FutureTask carrying result and exception back to the caller, and the shutdown-and-interrupt story - it assumes every primitive above at once.

02-Java-Core/Concurrency.readiness: This is a strong, genuinely above-average folder for the "make threads take turns" half of Java concurrency and a weak one for the "make a shared service safe under load" half. The 15 files cover the classic teaching sequence properly and with real depth: a visible data race against AtomicInteger, the instance-vs-class monitor question, wait/notify with a predicate, ReentrantLock with two Condition queues for targeted signalling, the odd/even and N-threads-modulo ordering puzzles, producer-consumer, CountDownLatch with a timed await, cooperative interrupt, ThreadLocal, a hand-rolled pool built from a BlockingQueue plus FutureTask, and a CompletableFuture fan-out/fan-in. Someone who can whiteboard all of that will clear a mid-level Java screen comfortably. The gap is that every problem here is a small synchronization exercise with a fixed, known set of threads, and none of them is the thing a staff interviewer actually reaches for, which is a shared component under concurrent load: no deadlock anywhere in the workspace (no two-lock inversion, no tryLock-with-timeout, no lock ordering), no ReentrantReadWriteLock or StampedLock (WriterReader looks like readers-writers but is a one-reader/one-writer ping-pong, so the read-mostly cache question is untouched), no Semaphore at all, no ConcurrentHashMap or computeIfAbsent in any Java-Core file, no CyclicBarrier or Phaser, and no CAS retry loop written by hand. The CompletableFuture work also stops at supplyAsync plus exceptionally plus a blocking join fan-in; thenCompose, thenCombine, allOf and timeouts appear nowhere, which matters a lot for a Spring/microservices-flavoured loop. Practically: he is interview-ready for the puzzle round and would likely stall on "here is a cache/pool/rate limiter, make it thread-safe and now tell me why it deadlocks." Closing the first five gaps below would move this folder from solid-mid to staff-credible, and they are mostly 40-to-80-line files in the same style as what is already there. Note that double-checked-locking singleton does not belong on the missing list: it already exists, correctly done with volatile plus reflection and serialization guards, at 03-LLD\Design-Patterns\1. Creational Design Patterns\Singleton.java, and it should stay there rather than be duplicated.

gaps.problem: Deadlock: reproduce it with two locks taken in opposite order, then fix it (global lock ordering, and tryLock with timeout plus backoff). Extend to Dining Philosophers.
gaps.technique: Lock-ordering deadlock, ReentrantLock.tryLock(timeout), livelock vs deadlock, jstack/ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads for detection
gaps.why: This is the single most-asked Java concurrency question after producer-consumer, and the word 'deadlock' does not appear in a single .java file anywhere in the workspace. The standard ask is 'write code that deadlocks' followed immediately by 'now fix it without removing either lock' - and the expected answer (impose a total order on lock acquisition, e.g. by System.identityHashCode when the two accounts are symmetric) is not something you derive on the spot. The bank-transfer variant (transfer(a,b) racing transfer(b,a)) is the usual framing at product companies. He has written plenty of two-lock-free code but never a two-lock hold-and-wait, so he has no muscle memory for the fix.

gaps.problem: Readers-writers: a concurrent key-value store or config cache where many readers run in parallel and a writer gets exclusive access.
gaps.technique: ReentrantReadWriteLock (read lock shared, write lock exclusive), lock downgrading, fair vs unfair and writer starvation, StampedLock optimistic reads as the follow-up
gaps.why: WriterReader.java has the right filename but is not this problem - it is a strict one-reader/one-writer alternation using two Conditions, which is a turn-taking puzzle. ReadWriteLock and StampedLock appear nowhere in the workspace. The interview version is 'this cache is read 95% of the time and synchronized is killing throughput, fix it', and the expected answer is a read/write lock plus a discussion of why you cannot upgrade a read lock to a write lock (instant deadlock) but can downgrade. Without this he will reach for synchronized or a single ReentrantLock and lose the read-concurrency point entirely.

gaps.problem: Make this cache thread-safe: a memoizing cache in front of a slow computation, then bound it as an LRU.
gaps.technique: ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent for atomic check-then-act, why get-then-put is a race that duplicates expensive work, CompletableFuture-valued map as the JCiP Memoizer, Collections.synchronizedMap vs ConcurrentHashMap, LinkedHashMap access-order LRU plus the lock
gaps.why: ConcurrentHashMap and computeIfAbsent do not appear in any 02-Java-Core file (only in DSA solutions, used single-threaded). This is the most common 'real code' concurrency question at product companies because it has a clean wrong answer everyone gives first: synchronize the whole method, or use get-then-put and not notice two threads both compute the same value. The staff-level follow-ups - why computeIfAbsent must not do long or recursive work while holding the bin lock, and why you store a Future rather than the value so the second caller waits instead of recomputing - are exactly the depth he is being screened for.

gaps.problem: Semaphore-bounded resource pool (N database connections, M concurrent callers) and a thread-safe token-bucket rate limiter.
gaps.technique: Semaphore acquire/release with try-finally, tryAcquire with timeout for fast-fail, permits vs a queue, refill arithmetic under a lock or via AtomicLong CAS
gaps.why: Semaphore appears nowhere in the workspace - it is the one core java.util.concurrent primitive he has zero exposure to, and it is the standard answer to any 'limit concurrency to N' question. The pairing matters at senior level: CountDownLatch (which he has) is one-shot and counts down to a gate, Semaphore is reusable and counts permits, and interviewers ask him to distinguish them. The rate limiter is the applied form and is a near-guaranteed question for a product company doing anything API-facing; the failure mode he should be able to name is releasing outside a finally so a thrown exception permanently leaks a permit.

gaps.problem: Async orchestration: call service A, feed its result into B, call C in parallel, combine all three, apply a per-call timeout and a fallback.
gaps.technique: thenCompose vs thenApply (flattening a nested future), thenCombine, allOf plus join for a typed fan-in, orTimeout/completeOnTimeout, supplying an explicit Executor instead of leaking onto ForkJoinPool.commonPool
gaps.why: MultiCSVProcessor does fan-out with supplyAsync and then blocks on join per future, and CompletableFutureExceptionHandling stops at exceptionally. thenCompose, thenCombine, allOf and orTimeout appear in zero files. thenApply-vs-thenCompose is one of the most frequently asked Java 8+ questions and the giveaway wrong answer is returning CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<T>>. The other point he currently cannot make is that supplyAsync without an executor runs on the common pool, so a blocking HTTP call there starves every parallel stream in the JVM - a standard senior follow-up in any Spring or microservices loop.

gaps.problem: Shut down a pool cleanly: drain in-flight work, cancel what is stuck, and enforce a per-task timeout.
gaps.technique: shutdown vs shutdownNow and the List<Runnable> it returns, awaitTermination in a two-phase loop, Future.cancel(true) vs get(timeout), invokeAll/invokeAny with a timeout, why shutdownNow only interrupts and cannot stop an uninterruptible task
gaps.why: StaticValChat busy-spins on isTerminated() to wait for completion, which is the tell that this is not internalised. He has awaitTermination elsewhere (CsvAppender, CsvReader, WorkFlowExecutor), so he is not starting from zero - hence medium, not high. But the specific things that get probed are the ones his code does not show: that shutdownNow hands back the queued tasks that never ran so you can log or requeue them, that the canonical pattern is shutdown then awaitTermination then shutdownNow then awaitTermination again, and that Future.cancel(true) only sets the interrupt flag so a task that ignores interrupts runs forever. This is asked as a follow-up to almost any executor question, which he will definitely be asked given CustomFutureThreadPool is on his list.

gaps.problem: Implement getAndIncrement yourself, then a lock-free stack with an AtomicReference head.
gaps.technique: compareAndSet retry loop, why the loop body must re-read the current value each attempt, AtomicReference for linked nodes, the ABA problem and AtomicStampedReference, LongAdder for high-contention counting
gaps.why: He has covered the theme 'AtomicInteger fixes the ++ race' but only as an API consumer - he calls getAndIncrement and getAndDecrement and has never written a do/while CAS loop. The standard staff follow-up to his own TwoThreadsToSingleValue is 'fine, now implement getAndIncrement without a lock', and the answer is a five-line retry loop that is hard to produce cold. The lock-free stack extends it to a linked structure and sets up ABA, and LongAdder is the practical answer to 'CAS under heavy contention spins and burns CPU - what do you use in a real counter?'. This is the difference between knowing the class and understanding CAS.

gaps.problem: Phase synchronization: N workers process a chunk, all wait at a barrier, a merge step runs, then the next round begins.
gaps.technique: CyclicBarrier with a barrier action, reuse across rounds, BrokenBarrierException, and as the deeper follow-up implementing your own CountDownLatch or Semaphore from wait/notify
gaps.why: CyclicBarrier and Phaser appear nowhere. 'CountDownLatch vs CyclicBarrier' is a stock question and his CountDownLatchDemo gives him only half the answer - he can say a latch counts down once and cannot be reused, but has never written the reusable barrier or hit BrokenBarrierException when one participant dies and the others hang forever. Iterative simulations and multi-round aggregation are the natural framing. The build-your-own-latch variant is the highest-signal version for staff level: it forces the generation counter and the while-loop predicate, and it ties directly back to the wait/notify work he has already done rather than being new material.

02-Java-Core/IO.techniques: Standard-input parsing with Scanner: token vs line reading, and the nextInt()/nextLine() buffer trap, Streaming a large file with BufferedReader so memory stays O(1) instead of O(file size), Fanning I/O work out to an ExecutorService, and why an unbounded submit loop needs backpressure (bounded queue) not a bigger pool, Serialising concurrent writes to one shared file: ReentrantLock vs a single-writer thread fed by a BlockingQueue, Throughput realities of file I/O: reopening a FileWriter per record, buffering, batching and flush/durability ordering, try-with-resources and correct lock release in finally as the baseline for every I/O routine

order.why: The smallest possible I/O primitive - open Scanner on System.in, read one token as int; everything else in the folder assumes you can do this without thinking.

order.technique: Scanner token loop, next vs nextInt
order.why: Extends the single read into a fixed-count token loop and sits exactly on the next()/nextInt()/nextLine() mixing trap, which is the first place naive input code breaks.

order.technique: BufferedReader streaming into a thread pool
order.why: First file-backed problem: streams line by line so memory stays flat, then hands each record to an ExecutorService with an AtomicLong counter - the read-side half of every large-file question, and the pattern CsvAppender's write side mirrors.

Hardest here because the obvious answer is wrong: 10 threads plus a global ReentrantLock and a FileWriter reopened per record serialise anyway and thrash the disk; the non-obvious insight is one writer thread behind a bounded queue with batched buffered writes, which you can only argue once CsvReader's streaming model is in place.

02-Java-Core/IO.readiness: This folder is deep on exactly one axis and empty on every other. The four files total under 7KB, and two of them (InputOutput, ScannerMain) are five-line Scanner demos. The real content is CsvReader/CsvAppender, and through them he has genuinely internalised the concurrency-and-throughput axis of file I/O: streaming with BufferedReader, fan-out to an ExecutorService, why an unbounded submit loop needs a bounded queue rather than more threads, lock-vs-single-writer-thread for one shared file, and the cost of reopening a FileWriter per record. That is a strong, senior-sounding story and it will carry the first ten minutes of an I/O question. What is missing is everything that is not about threads. There is no memory-bounded algorithm on a file at all — no top-K word count, no external merge sort — so the moment an interviewer says "the file is 200GB and the map does not fit in heap," he has nothing rehearsed. There is no encoding awareness: his own CsvReader opens with `new FileReader(CSV_FILE)` and CsvAppender writes with a bare `new FileWriter(...)`, both platform-default charset, which is the single easiest thing for a staff interviewer to pick at in code he wrote himself. There is no java.nio.file anywhere in the folder, which reads as pre-Java-7 muscle memory in 2026. And his CSV work never actually parses a CSV — it counts lines and concatenates strings, so the standard follow-up ("now a field contains a comma inside quotes") is unpracticed. Net: he would pass a mid-level I/O screen comfortably and stall on the senior/staff follow-ups, because the follow-ups all leave the concurrency axis he has covered. Four targeted problems (top-K, external sort, charset, NIO.2) would close most of the gap.

gaps.problem: Top-K frequent words in a large file (word-frequency counter with a bounded-memory follow-up)
gaps.technique: Stream with BufferedReader, split/normalise tokens, HashMap<String,Integer> counts, then a size-K min-heap for the top K. Follow-up: when the distinct-key set exceeds heap, shard by hash(word) % N into N spill files, count each shard independently, merge the per-shard top-Ks.
gaps.why: This is the single most-asked Java file-I/O coding problem at product companies, and it is the natural next question after 'read a big file line by line' — which is exactly where his CsvReader stops. He has the streaming half and none of the aggregation half. The sharding follow-up is the one that separates senior from mid: an interviewer who hears 'I'd just use a HashMap' and no answer to 'the map does not fit' will downgrade him regardless of how good his executor answer was.

gaps.problem: Sort a file larger than RAM (external merge sort)
gaps.technique: Read a fixed-size chunk, sort it in memory, write it to a temp file, repeat; then k-way merge the runs using a PriorityQueue of one BufferedReader-backed cursor per run, writing the merged output as a stream. Discuss run size vs merge fan-in, and deleting temp files in a finally/try-with-resources.
gaps.why: The canonical 'your data does not fit in memory' problem, and the one interviewers reach for when they want to see whether a candidate can keep memory O(chunk) instead of O(file). He already reasons in O(1)-memory terms for reading, which makes this a fair question to put to him — and right now he has no k-way-merge code anywhere in the folder. It also doubles as the practical answer to dedupe-a-huge-file and join-two-huge-files, so one problem buys three.

gaps.problem: Charset-correct read and write: byte streams vs character streams
gaps.technique: Replace FileReader/FileWriter with InputStreamReader/OutputStreamWriter over a FileInputStream/FileOutputStream with an explicit StandardCharsets.UTF_8, or Files.newBufferedReader(path, UTF_8). Show why FileReader uses the platform default charset, why a multi-byte UTF-8 character must never be split across a manually-managed byte[] buffer, and when you must stay on InputStream (binary) rather than Reader (text).
gaps.why: His own two CSV files use bare FileReader and FileWriter, so this is not a hypothetical gap — it is a defect sitting in the code he would screen-share. 'What charset does that FileReader use?' is a standard staff-level probe precisely because it is invisible on a dev laptop and corrupts data in production on a differently-configured host. He currently has no rehearsed answer for it, nor for the byte-stream-vs-char-stream distinction that the question always expands into.

gaps.problem: Modern file access with java.nio.file (NIO.2): Files, Path, Files.lines, directory walking
gaps.technique: Files.newBufferedReader / Files.lines with try-with-resources (the stream holds an open file handle and MUST be closed — the classic leak), Files.readAllLines vs Files.lines memory profile, Files.walk / Files.newDirectoryStream for recursive traversal, Files.size/exists/createDirectories, and StandardOpenOption for append and create-new.
gaps.why: There is zero java.nio.file in this folder — the only use in the whole repo is a single Files.list inside Concurrency/MultiCSVProcessor. Writing 2026 Java I/O entirely in java.io reads as dated to a staff interviewer, and 'rewrite this with Files.lines' is a routine warm-up. The specific trap they are fishing for is that Files.lines returns a resource-backed Stream which leaks a file descriptor unless it is closed, and that is not something he can reason out cold — it has to have been hit once.

gaps.problem: Java object serialization: Serializable, serialVersionUID, transient, custom writeObject/readObject
gaps.technique: ObjectOutputStream/ObjectInputStream round-trip of an object graph; what serialVersionUID does and what breaks when you omit it and evolve the class; transient fields and reinitialising them in readObject; why readResolve is needed to keep a singleton a singleton; and the argument for preferring JSON/protobuf on any wire that crosses a trust or version boundary.
gaps.why: Serialization is a textbook Java-core I/O topic and gets asked directly ('what is serialVersionUID', 'how do you exclude a field', 'how does serialization break a singleton'). His repo mentions it only as one line in a singleton note — he has never written a round-trip. The senior-level version of the question is the version-evolution failure (add a field, old bytes on disk, what happens) and the deserialization-of-untrusted-input risk; both need hands-on exposure to answer crisply rather than vaguely.

gaps.problem: Write a correct CSV parser: quoted fields, embedded commas and newlines, escaped quotes
gaps.technique: A small character-level state machine (IN_FIELD / IN_QUOTED / QUOTE_SEEN) instead of String.split(","), handling "" as an escaped quote and a record that legitimately spans multiple physical lines — which means the reader cannot assume one line equals one record. Then header-to-index mapping for named column access.
gaps.why: His CsvReader never parses anything; it counts lines, and CsvAppender builds rows by string concatenation with no quoting. The guaranteed follow-up to any CSV question is 'what if a field contains a comma' and then 'what if it contains a newline' — the second one invalidates his readLine-per-record loop entirely, which is an uncomfortable thing to discover live. It is also a clean, well-bounded 20-minute coding exercise, which is exactly why interviewers like it.

gaps.problem: Parallel processing of one large file by byte ranges (chunked split aligned to line boundaries)
gaps.technique: Divide file length into N ranges, seek each worker to its start with RandomAccessFile or SeekableByteChannel, skip forward to the next newline unless at offset 0, and read past the range end to finish the straddling record. Each worker produces a partial aggregate; the main thread merges them.
gaps.why: This is the correct answer to 'you have 8 cores and a 50GB file, how do you use them', and it is the direct counter to what his CsvReader actually does — submit one task per line, where the single-threaded reader is the bottleneck and the task overhead dwarfs the work. An interviewer looking at his code will ask exactly this, and 'add more threads to the pool' is the wrong answer. He knows the backpressure argument but not the partition-the-input argument.

gaps.problem: Crash-safe file update: write to temp, fsync, atomic rename
gaps.technique: Write the new content to a sibling temp file, force the data to disk (FileChannel.force / FileDescriptor.sync), close, then Files.move(tmp, target, ATOMIC_MOVE, REPLACE_EXISTING); fsync the parent directory if the rename itself must survive a crash. Contrast with truncate-and-rewrite-in-place, which leaves a half-written file if the process dies mid-write.
gaps.why: He has flush-vs-durability in his themes, which means an interviewer can legitimately push one step further: 'you flushed and the JVM was killed — what does the reader see?' Flushing alone does not save him; the readers-never-see-a-partial-file guarantee comes from atomic rename, and that is the point of the question. It is the standard mechanism behind config reloads, checkpoint files and log compaction, so it comes up in both coding and design rounds, and it is a short problem to practise relative to how often it pays off.

Self-contained java.time warm-up; teaches the formatter to OffsetDateTime to Instant chain before any time zone handling appears in harder problems.

02-Java-Core/Language-Features.readiness: This folder is unusually strong on the "second-order" Java topics that separate a senior candidate from a mid-level one — compile-time vs runtime dispatch, type erasure and the super-type-token trick, JDK dynamic proxies as the mechanism under Spring AOP, stream collectors beyond the basics, and lock-free updates on immutable snapshots. That is a genuinely impressive spread and it would carry him through the deeper half of a staff-level language round. The problem is that it is strong at the top and thin at the bottom: the fifteen problems here are heavily weighted toward exotica and mechanism, while several of the highest-frequency questions in any Java interview have no artifact at all. There is nothing on the equals/hashCode contract as it plays out in a HashMap (TreeSetRemoveExample covers the compareTo/equals divergence in a sorted set, which is a different mechanism), nothing on ConcurrentModificationException or the Arrays.asList / List.of mutation traps, nothing on string interning or the Integer cache, and his two generics files are a trivial <T> passthrough plus a Gson TypeToken — no wildcards, no PECS, no array covariance. He also has zero record or sealed-type code, only Q&A notes, which is a real exposure in 2026 when "model this value type" is a routine warm-up. The net effect is an odd risk profile: he is more likely to lose the interview in the first ten minutes on a question he considers beneath him than in the last twenty on proxies and erasure. Closing the five high-priority gaps below would take a few hours and would move this folder from "impressive but spiky" to genuinely interview-complete.

gaps.problem: EqualsHashCodeContractDemo — put an object into a HashMap/HashSet, mutate a field that hashCode() uses, then show get()/contains() returns null/false while the entry is still visible when iterating; plus the override-equals-but-not-hashCode variant and the getClass() vs instanceof symmetry question.

gaps.why: This is the single most-asked question in a Java interview and there is no artifact for it. TreeSetRemoveExample does contain a correct equals/hashCode pair, but it is exercising the compareTo/equals divergence in a sorted (red-black tree) structure — a completely different mechanism from hash bucketing. An interviewer probing the HashMap side would get nothing from his prep, and the follow-up ('why is a mutable key dangerous, what makes String a good key') is where senior candidates are separated from mid-level ones.

gaps.problem: ConcurrentModificationDemo — remove from a List while iterating with an enhanced for loop to trigger ConcurrentModificationException, then fix it three ways (Iterator.remove, removeIf, collect-then-removeAll); in the same file show Arrays.asList(...).add() throwing UnsupportedOperationException, List.of(null) throwing NPE, and a subList being a live view whose parent mutation invalidates it.

Arrays.asList appears four times across Streams.java and Java8StreamsCollectingAndThen.java but purely as a data producer — he has never been forced to confront that the thing it returns is a fixed-size view, not an ArrayList. Being asked 'you called add() on this and it blew up in prod, why' with no prior exposure is a plausible and avoidable loss.

gaps.problem: StringIdentityAndCache — compare literals, new String(), runtime-concatenated strings, compile-time constant expressions and intern() with both == and equals(); then the parallel Integer case: Integer.valueOf(127) == Integer.valueOf(127) is true but 128 is false, and Integer vs int comparison silently unboxing.

gaps.why: Tricky8.java touches String immutability only in the narrow sense of 'concat() without reassignment does nothing' — it never gets near identity, pooling or interning, and nothing anywhere touches the Integer cache. This pair is the classic opening whiteboard question at product companies precisely because it is cheap to ask and instantly reveals whether someone understands reference vs value semantics. There is no artifact here to fall back on.

gaps.problem: WildcardsAndPECS — write copy(List<? extends T> src, List<? super T> dst) and show why List<String> cannot be assigned to List<Object>; contrast with array covariance by storing an Integer into an Object[] that is really a String[] and catching ArrayStoreException; add a method pair that fails to compile due to erasure signature collision (List<String> vs List<Integer>).

gaps.problem: RecordsAndSealedTypes — reimplement the ImmutablePerson case as a record with a compact constructor that validates and defensively copies the list, show what the auto-generated equals/hashCode/toString actually do (and that the copy is still needed because records are only shallowly immutable), then model a small closed hierarchy with a sealed interface plus permits and switch over it exhaustively without a default branch.

gaps.problem: TryWithResourcesSemantics — a resource whose close() throws while the try body also throws, showing which exception propagates and recovering the other via getSuppressed(); two resources in one statement proving close order is reverse of declaration; and a finally block containing return that silently swallows an in-flight exception.

gaps.problem: Static factory methods and instance caching (Effective Java Item 1)
gaps.technique: Named creators such as of(), valueOf(), getInstance() replacing public constructors; returning a cached or interned instance instead of a new one; returning a subtype or interface the caller does not name; and the explicit comparison against the Factory pattern.
gaps.why: There is a specific Java interview question — 'what is the difference between a static factory method and the Factory design pattern' — that catches people who only learned GoF, and nothing in this folder addresses it. The answer is that a static factory is a language-level replacement for a constructor on the same class, while Factory Method is a structural delegation to a subclass. The caching angle also unlocks the Integer.valueOf and Boolean.valueOf questions, which are standard Java-fundamentals follow-ups, and it connects cleanly to the Flyweight file he already has next door.

gaps.problem: Prototype Registry — a manager holding pre-configured prototypes
gaps.technique: A Map<String, Prototype> of expensively-built, fully-configured template objects, where the client fetches by key and clones rather than constructing; used for document templates, game entities, or pre-loaded config objects.
gaps.why: His PrototypeExample clones one ad-hoc object, which shows the mechanism but not the motivation — it never explains why anyone would choose Prototype over just calling a constructor. The registry is the answer: when the configured state is expensive to assemble and you need many near-identical copies. Without it, the honest answer to 'when would you actually use Prototype in production' is thin, and that is the question that separates pattern recall from pattern judgement.

gaps.problem: Generic recursive builder for a class hierarchy (Effective Java Item 2)
gaps.technique: abstract static class Builder<T extends Builder<T>> with an abstract self() returning T, so that a subclass builder can inherit the parent's with-methods and still chain fluently without casting.
gaps.why: The near-guaranteed follow-up to any builder answer is 'now I subclass User into AdminUser with an extra field — does your builder still chain?' With his current static nested Builder it does not, because withFirstName() returns the parent Builder type and the subclass methods drop off the chain. The self-type trick is the standard fix and it is exactly the kind of Java-specific depth a staff-level Java interviewer uses to separate candidates who read Effective Java from ones who memorised a diagram.

gaps.problem: Replacing a singleton with dependency injection for testability
gaps.technique: Take a class that calls Singleton.getInstance() internally, show that it cannot be unit tested because the dependency cannot be substituted, then refactor to constructor injection with the singleton lifecycle owned by the container rather than the class; contrast a hand-rolled singleton with a Spring singleton-scoped bean (one instance per container, not per JVM).
gaps.why: He has the strongest singleton file in the folder but only covers how to build one, never when not to. The standard senior-level pivot after a good singleton answer is 'fine — now how do you test a class that depends on it', and the expected answer is that you do not, you inject it. The Spring contrast matters too: a singleton-scoped bean is per-ApplicationContext while a static getInstance() is per-classloader, and conflating the two is a common and visible mistake in Spring-heavy interviews.

03-LLD/Design-Patterns/2. Structural Pat.techniques: Wrap-and-delegate: hold a reference to another object and forward calls — the single primitive underneath Adapter, Decorator, Proxy and Facade, Same-interface wrapping: when the wrapper implements the wrapped type, wrappers stack recursively (Decorator chain) and become drop-in substitutes (Proxy), Composition over inheritance: avoiding the combinatorial subclass explosion, either by stacking wrappers (Decorator) or by splitting one hierarchy into two (Bridge), Uniform interface over part-whole structures: treating a leaf and a container identically so client code recurses without type checks (Composite), Intent vs structure: Adapter, Decorator and Proxy are near-identical in code and differ only in purpose — being able to say which one you are using and why is the interview signal, Indirection as a control point: a wrapper is where you put access control, lazy initialisation, caching, logging and remoting without touching the real class (Proxy, the basis of Spring AOP and Hibernate lazy loading), State partitioning for memory: splitting intrinsic (shared, cached by a factory) from extrinsic (per-instance, passed in) state (Flyweight), Subsystem encapsulation: one coarse entry point that orchestrates several fine-grained services, the everyday shape of a service-layer facade

order.why: The atom of every other file here — hold a reference to an incompatible object, implement the interface the client expects, translate in between; Decorator, Proxy, Facade and Bridge are all variations on this one move.

order.technique: One entry point over a subsystem
order.why: The degenerate case of delegation — aggregate several collaborators, no shared interface, no polymorphism — so it is the easiest warm-up and nothing later depends on it, but it is also the pattern you already write daily as a service layer.

Takes Adapter's delegation and adds the key constraint — the wrapper implements the same interface as the wrappee — which is what makes wrappers stack; this recursion is the idea Proxy and Composite both assume.

Structurally identical to Decorator, so it must come after it; the new content is intent and lifecycle — the wrapper owns creation (lazy init) and gates calls, which is exactly how Spring AOP and Hibernate lazy loading work under a Java staff interview.

Generalises the linear wrapper chain into a tree — a node holds many children rather than one wrappee — and adds the transparency-vs-safety trade-off of where add/remove lives, which is the follow-up interviewers actually push on.

Assumes Composite's context-object-referencing-shared-object shape and adds the memory insight: cache the invariant part in a factory, pass the varying part per call — mechanical once seen, but the state split is the part candidates miss.

Hardest here because the insight is upstream of the code — recognising two orthogonal dimensions of change and refusing the cartesian-product subclass explosion — and because you must defend why it is not just Strategy or Adapter, which only lands after both of those are solid.

03-LLD/Design-Patterns/2. Structural Pat.readiness: Pattern coverage here is complete — all seven GoF structural patterns are present (Adapter, Bridge, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Flyweight, Proxy), each implemented correctly and idiomatically with a clear intent comment at the top. That clears the screening bar: if an interviewer asks "explain Decorator and code it", he is fine. The weakness is that every file is the same artifact — a 40-90 line single-file textbook demo in a toy domain (coffee with milk, trees on a map, a product bundle, online-vs-instore payment) with no JDK or framework grounding, no concurrency or lifecycle concerns, and no problem statement ambiguous enough that he has to *choose* a pattern rather than illustrate a named one. Senior and staff loops rarely ask "implement Decorator"; they ask "how does @Transactional actually work and why does calling it from within the same class do nothing", "add retries and caching to this client without touching it", "we're integrating three payment gateways, design the boundary", "design an in-memory file system" — and they score the follow-ups: intent discrimination, thread-safety, unbounded growth, ordering, what happens when the wrapped type can't satisfy the wrapper's contract. He has the vocabulary and none of the war stories. Two concrete tells a staff interviewer would seize on: ProxyDesignPattern.java is a hand-written static proxy with no mention of java.lang.reflect.Proxy or CGLIB, and FlyweightExample.java's factory is a plain static HashMap with computeIfAbsent — not thread-safe, unbounded, and never cleaned up, which is exactly the question that follows "nice, now put this in a web server". Fixing the eight gaps below is mostly a matter of re-staging patterns he already knows onto harder problems, so this is maybe two to three evenings of work, not a rebuild.

gaps.problem: Annotation-driven dynamic proxy: implement @Transactional / @Retry / @Audit using java.lang.reflect.Proxy + InvocationHandler, then explain the CGLIB subclass variant
gaps.technique: JDK dynamic proxy vs CGLIB subclass proxy; InvocationHandler.invoke dispatch; proxy-creation factory; the self-invocation problem (an internal this.method() call bypasses the proxy); why final and private methods can't be advised; interface-based vs class-based proxying trade-offs
gaps.why: ProxyDesignPattern.java is a hand-written static proxy — one class, one interface, compile-time. Every Java backend interview at senior level asks some form of 'how does Spring AOP / @Transactional actually work under the hood', and the expected answer is dynamic proxying, plus the self-invocation gotcha that causes real production bugs. He currently has no code and no vocabulary for reflection-based proxying, so he would give the static-proxy answer and get marked down as textbook-only. This is the single highest-return gap in the folder.

gaps.problem: Design an in-memory file system: mkdir, addFile, ls, du (recursive size), find by name/glob, and path resolution from a string like /a/b/c.txt
gaps.technique: Composite with a mutation API; the GoF safety-vs-transparency decision (do add/remove live on Component so clients are uniform, or only on Directory so leaves can't be misused?); parent back-pointers; recursive accumulators vs an explicit stack; iterator over a tree; guarding against cycles when symlinks/hard links enter
gaps.why: CompositePattern.java only does read-only recursion — sum the prices, print the tree. It never asks the questions that make Composite interesting: where do add/remove live, how do you walk to an arbitrary path, how do you iterate lazily. 'Design a file system' or 'design a folder/document hierarchy' is one of the most frequently asked LLD prompts at product companies, and the follow-up is always safety-vs-transparency. He can build the tree; he would stall on the API-design trade-off, which is the part being scored.

gaps.problem: Build a java.io-style stream decorator stack (Buffered -> Gzip -> Counting -> Encrypting over a base stream), then produce an inventory of structural patterns in the JDK and Spring and defend each mapping
gaps.technique: Decorator over a real abstract base class rather than a toy interface; wrapping semantics for close()/flush() propagation; JDK/Spring mapping — java.io streams and Collections.unmodifiableList (Decorator), Arrays.asList and InputStreamReader (Adapter), java.awt.Container and Spring Security filter chain (Composite), SLF4J and JdbcTemplate (Facade), Integer.valueOf cache and String pool (Flyweight), JDBC DriverManager/Driver and SLF4J-over-bindings (Bridge), Hibernate lazy-loading proxies (Proxy)
gaps.why: Every file in the folder uses an invented domain, and the standard interviewer probe after any pattern answer is 'where have you seen this in a library you actually use?'. Answering 'coffee with milk' at senior level signals memorised-not-applied. There is no JDK or Spring reference anywhere in these seven files. This is cheap to close and it upgrades the quality of every other answer he gives, because each pattern then comes with a real citation instead of a cartoon.

gaps.problem: Wrap a service call in a resilience middleware chain — caching, retry with backoff, circuit breaker, rate limiter, metrics, logging — assembled from configuration rather than hard-coded
gaps.technique: Same-interface decorators composed in a deliberate order; why order changes behaviour (retry inside vs outside the circuit breaker, cache above vs below retry); builder or list-driven chain assembly; where the chain leaks (exception types must survive each layer, equals/hashCode break, callers who need the concrete underlying type, unwrapping helpers); comparison against an interceptor/filter chain and against AOP
gaps.why: DecoratorDesignPattern.java stacks two decorators whose order is irrelevant — milk then sugar costs the same as sugar then milk, so it never teaches the one thing that matters industrially. 'Add retries and caching to this client without modifying it' is a standard senior LLD prompt, and the discriminating follow-up is 'does retry go inside or outside the breaker, and why'. He knows the mechanics of stacking; he has not confronted ordering semantics or where a decorator chain becomes a liability.

gaps.problem: Design the integration boundary for three third-party providers behind one internal port — e.g. Razorpay, Stripe and PayPal behind a single PaymentProcessor, or three SMS/email vendors behind one Notifier
gaps.technique: Adapter at production scale (ports-and-adapters / hexagonal); translating each vendor's error model, status codes and idempotency semantics into one internal contract; handling capability mismatch when an adaptee genuinely cannot do what the port promises (fail fast, emulate, or narrow the port); a registry or factory that selects the adapter; keeping vendor DTOs from leaking into the domain; testing with a fake adapter
gaps.why: AdapterPatternDemo.java adapts CSV text to JSON — a pure format conversion with no failure modes, one adaptee, and no error semantics. The real interview version is 'we're adding a second payment gateway, how do you structure it', and the hard question is what you do when provider B has no equivalent for an operation provider A supports. That capability-mismatch question separates people who have shipped an integration from people who have read the pattern. He would draw the right box and then have nothing to say about the mismatch.

gaps.problem: Harden a Flyweight factory for production: make the pool thread-safe, bounded and reclaimable, then explain how it differs from a cache and from Singleton
gaps.technique: ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent vs synchronized vs double-checked locking; why intrinsic state must be immutable for sharing to be safe; bounded pools with LRU eviction; WeakHashMap or SoftReference to allow reclamation; measuring the actual memory win; walking through Integer.valueOf's -128..127 cache and the == vs equals trap it creates
gaps.why: FlyweightExample.java's factory is a static HashMap mutated via computeIfAbsent with no synchronisation and no eviction — it is a data race and an unbounded leak in any multi-threaded server. A staff interviewer will spot that in ten seconds and ask 'what happens under concurrent load', and 'how is this different from just a cache' is the standard next question. He has the state-partitioning concept correct; he has not been asked to run it in a real process.

gaps.problem: Intent-discrimination drill: take one interface and write five wrappers around it — Adapter, Decorator, Proxy, Facade and a Bridge split — then defend which is which and when you would pick each
gaps.technique: Naming the distinguishing question for each intent (Adapter changes the interface, Decorator adds behaviour behind the same interface, Proxy controls access behind the same interface, Facade simplifies a subsystem, Bridge splits one hierarchy into two); the three classic confusions — Bridge vs Strategy, Facade vs Mediator, Decorator vs Proxy; class adapter (inheritance) vs object adapter (composition) and why composition wins in Java
gaps.why: His theme notes already say intent-vs-structure is the interview signal, so he knows this matters — but the folder has seven files each demonstrating one pattern in isolation, never side by side, and 'Bridge vs Strategy' and 'Facade vs Mediator' appear nowhere. Interviewers deliberately describe an ambiguous requirement and watch which pattern you name and whether you can justify it against its two nearest neighbours. Recognising patterns one at a time does not prove you can discriminate between them under pressure.

gaps.problem: Design a rule or discount engine: composable conditions (AND / OR / NOT / leaf predicates) evaluated over an order, with a readable builder for expressing rules
gaps.technique: Composite over boolean expressions rather than numeric aggregation; short-circuit evaluation inside composite nodes; a fluent builder or small DSL for rule construction; serialising a rule tree to and from JSON so rules are data rather than code; keeping evaluation side-effect free
gaps.why: This is Composite's second and harder shape — a tree whose nodes decide rather than accumulate — and 'design a discount engine' or 'design a fraud-rule evaluator' is a common product-company LLD prompt. CompositePattern.java covers only the accumulate shape, where every child is visited unconditionally. Lower priority than the file system because a strong file-system answer transfers most of the way here, but it is the version most likely to show up in an e-commerce or fintech interview.

03-LLD/Design-Patterns/3. Behavioral Pat.techniques: Delegation to an interface vs. inheritance hooks — the two axes of varying behavior (Strategy vs. Template Method), the single most-asked LLD trade-off question, Event notification and decoupled communication — one-to-many broadcast (Observer) generalizing into an N-to-N hub (Mediator), the backbone of pub/sub, listeners and chat/notification LLD rounds, Behavior as an object — requests (Command), states (State) and snapshots (Memento) reified into first-class classes so they can be queued, swapped, logged or undone, Replacing if/else and switch chains with polymorphism — State for lifecycle machines, Chain of Responsibility for handle-or-forward pipelines (servlet filters, Spring Security, approval flows, ATM dispensers), Separating traversal and operations from the data structure — Iterator for traversal, Visitor for double dispatch over a fixed type hierarchy, Interpreter for recursive evaluation of a composite AST, Open/Closed in practice: which axis stays open — Strategy/Chain keep algorithms open, Visitor keeps operations open at the cost of freezing the type set (the trade-off staff interviewers probe)

order.why: The root primitive of the whole folder — Command, State and Chain are all Strategy with a twist, so nothing else reads cleanly until 'inject behavior as an object' is automatic.
The inheritance-based counterpart to Strategy; learned immediately after it so the classic 'Strategy vs Template Method, which and why' question has a real answer rather than a definition.

The second primitive — register/remove/notify is assumed by Mediator later and by every event-driven LLD prompt (notifications, stock ticker, cache invalidation), so it belongs before the medium tier.
Easiest file here and the gentlest warm-up: a hasNext/next cursor holding its own index, and the first taste of 'pull behavior out of the collection' that Visitor pushes much further.
Strategy plus a bound receiver, so it must follow Strategy; easy as written (invoker + concrete commands, no undo) but must-know because it unlocks undo/redo, macros, job queues and CQRS.

order.technique: Encapsulated state snapshot on a stack
order.why: Sits right after Command because the two combine into the standard undo/redo answer; on its own it is just originator/memento/caretaker with a Stack.

First real medium problem and the highest-frequency LLD machine question (order lifecycle, vending machine, elevator); assumes Strategy, then adds the non-trivial step of a state choosing its own successor.
Medium because each handler must decide partial-handle vs. forward with a remainder; not marked must-know only because 12 years of servlet filters and Spring Security already teach the shape.
Placed last in the medium tier because it is Observer generalized to many-to-many, and the real lesson — hub vs. mesh coupling, and the god-object risk — only lands once Observer and Chain are owned.
The first genuinely non-obvious insight: accept(this) exists purely to recover the concrete type, and the pattern trades a frozen type hierarchy for open-ended operations.

order.technique: Recursive evaluation of a composite AST
order.why: Capstone — the only file with no description comment and the rarest pattern; assumes the composite tree plus recursive evaluation, and is where a grammar gets mapped onto terminal/non-terminal classes.

03-LLD/Design-Patterns/3. Behavioral Pat.readiness: On taxonomy this folder is complete: all 11 GoF behavioral patterns are present, one runnable, commented example each (C:\Users\Ravi Varma Chaluvadi\AppData\Roaming\JetBrains\IdeaIC2025.2\scratches\AAScratches\03-LLD\Design-Patterns\3. Behavioral Patterns), and nothing canonical is missing at the pattern level — for a screening round that asks "explain Strategy vs Template Method" or "which pattern fits this?", he is ready. The gap is depth and composition, which is exactly what separates a senior pass from a staff pass. Every file is 68-171 lines of single-pattern, single-thread, happy-path demo in a toy domain (TV remote, weather station, playlist, ATM dispenser): CommandDesignPattern.java has no undo(), no history stack and no macro command despite its own header advertising undoable operations; ObserverDesignPattern.java notifies from a plain ArrayList with no thread safety, no exception isolation and no async delivery; IteratorPatternExample.java hand-rolls its own Iterator interface and never touches java.util.Iterable, fail-fast modCount or remove(); StateDesignPatternExample.java models a linear order lifecycle with no illegal-transition handling and no state-owned data. None of the eleven files composes two patterns, and the Problems folder next door holds only ParkingLotExample.java and TicTacToe.java — so there is nowhere in the workspace where State, Strategy and Observer are made to coexist under one requirement set. In a 45-minute round the question is almost never "show me Command"; it is "design undo/redo", "design a vending machine", "design the notification fan-out" — and every one of those dies on the first follow-up about concurrency, failure, memory or illegal input rather than on the pattern itself. Roughly a weekend of work on the four high-priority items below closes most of it, because the pattern vocabulary is already there.

gaps.problem: Undo/Redo in a text editor — Command objects that carry their own undo(), an undo stack plus a redo stack, and a MacroCommand that groups several edits into one undoable unit
gaps.technique: Command with reversible operations + Composite Command, contrasted against Memento snapshots
gaps.why: CommandDesignPattern.java stops at execute() on a TV remote — there is no undo(), no history, no invoker-side stack, and MementoDesignPattern.java only pops a single undo stack with no redo. 'Design undo/redo' is the single most-asked Command question, and the whole interview lives in the follow-up: inverse-operation commands are cheap but hard to write correctly, full-state mementos are trivial but blow up memory on a large document, and the senior answer is the hybrid (commands for small edits, periodic snapshots for checkpoints) plus what happens to the redo stack when a new edit arrives. He currently has the two halves as separate toy files and has never had to reconcile them.

gaps.problem: An event bus / notification hub that survives production — 10k subscribers, subscribe and unsubscribe while a notify is in flight, one slow or throwing listener, and listeners that outlive their owners
gaps.technique: Observer hardened: CopyOnWriteArrayList or snapshot-then-iterate, per-listener try/catch, executor-backed async delivery, WeakReference registration, push vs pull payloads
gaps.why: ObserverDesignPattern.java iterates a plain ArrayList and calls update() inline, so an unsubscribe inside a callback throws ConcurrentModificationException, one listener throwing kills the rest of the fan-out, and one slow listener blocks the publisher. Every interviewer who sees a correct Observer immediately asks those three questions, and the memory-leak one (a registered listener is a strong reference, which is why Swing and Spring listener leaks exist) is the staff-level probe. He has the shape but none of the hardening, and this same machinery is what a 'design a notification service' or 'design a stock ticker' round is actually grading.

gaps.problem: A real custom iterator — a lazy nested/flattening iterator over a list-of-lists or an in-order BST iterator, implementing java.util.Iterator<T> and java.lang.Iterable<T> so it works in a for-each, with fail-fast modCount and a working remove()
gaps.technique: Iterator implementing the JDK contract, external vs internal iteration, lazy advancement with O(h) space
gaps.why: IteratorPatternExample.java declares its own Iterator interface over an ArrayList index — it never implements java.util.Iterator, so the class cannot be used in an enhanced for loop, and it has no remove(), no modCount, and nothing lazy. The asked versions of this problem are all lazy: flatten a nested list without materialising it, iterate a BST in order using O(height) space, merge or zip two iterators. The follow-ups are the JDK contract itself — what hasNext() must guarantee about side effects, why ArrayList throws ConcurrentModificationException and how modCount produces that, and why Iterator.remove() is the only safe mutation during traversal. This is also the closest behavioural pattern to a coding round, so it gets asked in both LLD and DSA interviews.

gaps.problem: Vending machine (or ATM) as a hardened state machine — money and inventory owned by the context, guarded transitions, explicit rejection of illegal events (insert coin while DISPENSING, select while NO_MONEY), refund on cancel, and a documented transition table
gaps.technique: State with context-owned data, plus the design decision of where transitions live (inside each state vs a central table) and Strategy for the payment mode
gaps.why: This is not a duplicate of StateDesignPatternExample.java: that file is a linear NEW->PAID->SHIPPED->DELIVERED walk where every event is legal and the state objects hold no data. The vending machine is the version interviewers actually name, and it fails on the parts he has never written — what an invalid event does (silently ignore, throw, or return a typed result), where the accumulated coins and stock counts live so states stay stateless and shareable, how cancel unwinds a partial transaction, and whether transitions belong in the state classes (open to new states, scattered) or in a central map (auditable, closed). The transition table is also the artifact a staff interviewer asks him to draw before any code.

gaps.problem: Selecting a strategy at runtime without reintroducing the if/else — a strategy registry keyed by type, self-registering implementations, and the Spring idiom of injecting List<Strategy> or Map<String, Strategy>
gaps.technique: Strategy + registry/lookup map, ServiceLoader, Spring's collection injection and @Qualifier
gaps.why: StrategyDesignPattern.java news up CreditCardPayment and PayPalPayment directly in main, which sidesteps the question every interviewer asks next: Strategy removed the switch from the algorithm but something still has to pick, so where did the switch go? The expected answer is that the branch collapses into a Map<PaymentType, PaymentStrategy> built once, that Spring can populate it by injecting every bean of the interface type, and that a new strategy then ships without touching the selector — which is what makes the Open/Closed claim true rather than rhetorical. He already reasons about which axis stays open; he has not written the registry that delivers it, and this is the most common way a clean Strategy answer still loses points.

gaps.problem: A request pipeline / interceptor chain — ordered filters (auth, rate limit, validation, logging) where any handler can short-circuit with a response, ordering is explicit, and handlers can act both before and after the downstream call
gaps.technique: Chain of Responsibility in its middleware form: list-driven chain assembly, short-circuit return, around-style pre/post hooks
gaps.why: ChainOfResponsibilityExample.java is an ATM dispenser, which is the atypical case — every handler partially handles and always forwards, so it never exercises the pattern's real decision, which is 'handle and stop'. The asked shape is the servlet/Spring Security filter chain: handlers return a result or veto the request, the chain is assembled from an ordered list rather than hand-wired setNext calls, and a handler needs to run code after the rest of the chain completes (timing, logging, response rewriting), which a naive linked chain cannot do. Since his themes already name servlet filters and Spring Security as the motivating examples, being unable to build one when asked is a visible gap.

gaps.problem: Elevator / lift system for one building — one composite design where State (idle/moving/doors-open), Strategy (FCFS vs SCAN/LOOK scheduling) and Observer (floor displays, door sensors) all have to coexist
gaps.technique: Multi-pattern composition, with the pattern boundaries justified rather than assumed
gaps.why: Nothing in this folder or in the Problems folder (only ParkingLotExample.java and TicTacToe.java) composes two behavioural patterns, yet every senior LLD round is a system prompt, not a pattern prompt. Elevator is the canonical one because it forces the exact judgement staff interviewers grade: which varying thing is a state and which is a strategy (direction is state, request scheduling is strategy), who owns the request queue, how a pluggable scheduler is compared against a fixed one, and how displays are updated without the controller knowing about them. Knowing eleven patterns individually does not produce that decomposition under time pressure — one rehearsed composite does.

order.technique: Grid state with incremental win check
order.why: The primitive every board/grid LLD assumes — encapsulate mutable state behind one validated move() API and check only the affected row/col/diagonal; ParkingLot's entity-and-state-transition modeling is this idea scaled up.

gaps.problem: Elevator / Lift Control System (multi-car)
gaps.technique: Split fleet-level ElevatorController from per-car Elevator; each car holds a direction + state machine (IDLE/MOVING_UP/MOVING_DOWN/DOORS_OPEN) and a sorted set of stops; dispatch policy behind an interface (nearest-car, then SCAN/LOOK) so the interviewer can swap it.

His parking lot picks the first matching spot — that is a search, not a scheduling policy, so he has never had to defend an algorithm choice ('why nearest-car, and when does it starve?'). Every follow-up here (external vs internal request, a car already moving past the floor, all cars busy) is unrehearsed for him.

gaps.problem: Movie Ticket Booking / Seat Reservation (BookMyShow style)
gaps.technique: Two-phase reservation: a temporary hold with a TTL plus an expiry sweep, then an idempotent confirm; lock granularity chosen per show rather than globally; booking state machine (HELD -> CONFIRMED -> CANCELLED / EXPIRED) with payment as a separate concern.
gaps.why: This is the canonical concurrency LLD, and his only concurrency artefact is `synchronized parkVehicle` — the coarse baseline he already knows does not scale but has never replaced. The interviewer's whole follow-up branch (two users click the same seat simultaneously; a user abandons checkout and the seat must return; why lock the show and not the whole theatre) has no rehearsed answer in this folder.

gaps.problem: Splitwise / Expense Sharing
gaps.technique: Split strategy as a first-class validated object (EQUAL / EXACT / PERCENTAGE, shares must sum to the total), a balance ledger keyed by an ordered user pair with a signed amount, and a settlement pass that simplifies debts down to a minimal transfer set.
gaps.why: The most common 'model this business domain' LLD at product companies, and the modelling shape — a directed graph of net balances — appears nowhere in his folder, which is all containment hierarchies (Lot -> Floor -> Spot). Candidates most often fail on two specific things he has not practised: validating that the split adds up at creation time, and keeping the *sign/direction* of a debt straight, which is precisely the boundary-correctness bug class he already got caught by with the reversed Duration.between.

gaps.problem: API Rate Limiter (token bucket + sliding window, per client)
gaps.technique: Algorithm behind a RateLimiter interface so token-bucket, fixed-window and sliding-window-log are swappable; lazy refill computed from timestamps on each call instead of a background thread; a per-key bucket map with fine-grained locking or CAS; clock injected so it is testable without sleeps.
gaps.why: Asked as a standalone senior LLD round and as the follow-up to almost any API design question, and it is the natural place for him to *finally implement* the 'why coarse synchronized does not scale' point he has only noted. The LoggerRateLimiter in his DSA folder does not count — it is the LeetCode 'print a message at most once per 10 seconds' puzzle, with no pluggable algorithm, no per-client buckets, and no concurrency.

gaps.problem: Vending Machine (or ATM)
gaps.technique: State as objects — IdleState, HasMoneyState, DispensingState, OutOfStockState — where each state owns which transitions are legal and returns the next state, plus inventory tracking and a change/denomination computation that can fail.
gaps.why: This is the textbook State-pattern problem and the interviewer's standard escalation is 'your enum + switch is growing; convert it to state objects' — the exact conversion he has never performed, since both his problems use an enum as a passive flag and his StateDesignPatternExample is pattern-in-isolation, not a state machine he chose under pressure. It also forces the 'what if the machine cannot make exact change' path, where candidates discover their transitions are not total.

gaps.problem: Chess (or any piece-hierarchy board game)
gaps.technique: Polymorphic move validation — Piece.canMove(board, from, to) overridden per piece — with Board as a real object, Move objects recorded in a history for undo, and game-termination checks kept separate from move application.
gaps.why: His TicTacToe is a win-checker, not an object model: no Board, Player or Game class, no turn enforcement, no rejection of an occupied cell, no draw. Chess is where interviewers test class hierarchy and open/closed ('add a new piece without touching the engine') — and he needs one game problem where the design, not the O(n) trick, is the answer, because the incremental-check optimisation he knows well is worth about two minutes of a forty-five-minute round.

gaps.problem: Notification / Alerting Dispatch Service
gaps.technique: Observer for subscriber fan-out, channel Strategy (email / SMS / push) chosen per user preference, and a Chain of Responsibility or decorator stack for dedupe, throttle and retry with backoff; templates rendered separately from delivery.
gaps.why: Nothing in the folder has a one-to-many event flow, yet 'how does the rest of the system find out the spot was freed / the seat was booked?' is a standard extension on every allocation problem he has done, and the expected answer is a publisher with registered listeners. It is also the cheapest way to practise keeping a slow, failure-prone side effect off the critical path of a state transition — a point a staff-level interviewer will push on.

gaps.problem: Logging Framework (levels, appenders, async)
gaps.technique: Level filtering plus a chain of handlers, an Appender abstraction (console / file / rolling file), singleton-ish configuration loaded once, and an async mode with a bounded queue, a consumer thread and a flush on shutdown.
gaps.why: A common Java-backend warm-up LLD, and the async variant reuses his bounded-queue work from WorkFlowExecutor while adding the shutdown/flush ordering problem that trips people up. Marked low because he can assemble most of this from his existing Chain-of-Responsibility and Singleton examples — the gap is real but it is the one he is most likely to survive cold.

04-HLD-System-Design/code.techniques: Distributed unique ID generation (bit packing, custom epoch, clock skew, sequence overflow), NoSQL wide-column data modelling (keyspace, column family, row key, wide rows for time-series), Replica reconciliation and anti-entropy (hash trees, cheap divergence detection), Durability vs storage cost (replication vs erasure coding, XOR parity, Reed-Solomon), Cryptographic hashing as a system-design primitive (SHA-256, integrity proofs)

order.why: Identity comes first: sharding, sort order and keyset pagination in every later design assume a unique monotonic key already exists.
The store those IDs are written into — partition-key plus clustering-column thinking that every Cassandra or DynamoDB answer later leans on.
Assumes replicated rows already exist (from the wide-column model); teaches cheap detection of which subtree diverged before you discuss repairing it.
Last because it only makes sense once 3x replication is the assumed baseline; the parity-algebra insight buying the same durability at ~1.5x overhead is non-obvious.

04-HLD-System-Design/code.readiness: This folder is about 25% of the way to staff-ready, and its four problems cluster suspiciously tightly: Snowflake, wide-column, Merkle and erasure coding are essentially four pages of the Dynamo/Cassandra paper — ID generation, data model, anti-entropy, durability. That is a coherent theme, but it means a single interviewer probe in the same territory ("how do keys get assigned to nodes in the first place?") lands on empty space, because the partitioner — consistent hashing — is the one Dynamo pillar he has not written. The other structural gap is that everything here is a write-path or storage primitive; there is no code at all for the request-path primitives every product-company loop opens with (rate limiting, idempotency, caching under concurrency, backpressure), even though his notes folder discusses Saga, payments and quorum at length. Quality is also uneven in a way an interviewer will catch on the first follow-up: MerkleTreeExample computes a root but has no tree-diff or proof-verification, so it cannot actually do the job Merkle trees exist for (comparing two replicas to locate divergent key ranges) — he can explain the idea but not demonstrate it; ErasureCodingExample is XOR-only with a single parity, so it dies on the standard "now lose two of six fragments" follow-up; WideColumnStore is a nested HashMap with no sorted clustering columns, no partitioning and no flush/compaction path, so "walk me through what Cassandra does on disk" has no code behind it. Net: he can hold a 20-minute conversation about replication and storage, but he currently could not whiteboard a partitioner, a limiter, a conflict resolver or an idempotent write — and those are the four things most likely to be asked.

gaps.problem: Consistent hashing ring with virtual nodes
gaps.technique: TreeMap/sorted ring of hash positions, N virtual nodes per physical node, successor lookup via ceilingEntry, add/remove node and report which keys move
gaps.why: This is the single most-asked HLD coding primitive and the one hole that his existing set makes glaring. He has the Dynamo data model (WideColumnStore), the anti-entropy (Merkle) and the durability story (erasure coding) but not the partitioner that decides which node owns a key. Any interviewer who hears 'wide-column store' will ask 'how do you map a partition key to a node, and what happens when you add the 9th node?' Modulo hashing reshuffles nearly everything; the expected answer is a ring with ~100-200 vnodes per node plus a demonstration that only 1/N of keys move. He also needs the vnode rationale (load smoothing and parallel rebuild on node loss), which only lands if he has written the ring.

gaps.problem: Distributed rate limiter (token bucket + sliding-window counter)
gaps.technique: Token bucket with lazy refill computed from elapsed time, sliding-window log and sliding-window counter variants, per-key limiter map, then the distributed version using an atomic check-and-decrement (Redis INCR/EXPIRE or a Lua script) with a note on why GET-then-SET races
gaps.why: Tied with consistent hashing as the most common request-path coding ask, and it is genuinely absent. He has LoggerRateLimiter and HitCounter in 01-DSA/19, but those are LeetCode framings: one is a fixed-window per-message gate, the other a 300-second hit count, and neither involves burst allowance, refill rate, or multi-instance coordination. The interview version is 'API gateway, 10k req/s, 20 app servers, per-customer quota' — that needs token bucket for burst semantics and an explicit answer on where the counter lives and how two servers avoid both letting a request through. Without code he will hand-wave the atomicity, which is exactly the part being tested.

gaps.problem: Bloom filter (with false-positive math and a counting variant)
gaps.technique: Bit array plus k independent hashes derived by double hashing, sizing from m = -n*ln(p)/(ln2)^2 and k = (m/n)*ln2, measured false-positive rate, counting Bloom filter for deletes
gaps.why: The canonical 'save an expensive lookup' primitive and a direct follow-up to work he already has. Cassandra keeps a Bloom filter per SSTable precisely so a read can skip disk; he has written a wide-column store and will be asked how reads avoid touching every file. It is also the standard answer to 'is this username taken', 'have we seen this URL', and cache-penetration questions. What gets probed is not the bit array but whether he can pick m and k from an expected n and target p, and state clearly that false positives are possible while false negatives are not — and that deletes are impossible without the counting variant. That is a 25-minute exercise he has not done.

gaps.problem: Vector clocks / version vectors with conflict detection and resolution
gaps.technique: Map of nodeId to counter per value, increment on local write, merge on replication, compare for descends-from / concurrent, surface siblings, then contrast with last-write-wins on a physical timestamp and with Lamport clocks
gaps.why: This is the exact next question after his Merkle tree and he has nothing for it. The Merkle tree tells you two replicas differ; the interviewer's immediate follow-up is 'you found a divergent key — now which value wins?' The expected answer distinguishes a genuine causal update (one version dominates, take it) from a true concurrent write (versions are incomparable, so you either keep siblings like Dynamo, or drop data with LWW). He also needs this to answer 'why is last-write-wins dangerous under clock skew', which connects straight back to the clock-skew branch he already wrote in SnowflakeIdGenerator. Writing the comparison logic is the only way the concurrent-vs-causal distinction becomes sayable under pressure.

gaps.problem: Idempotency key store and transactional outbox (exactly-once effects)
gaps.technique: Idempotency-key table with a unique constraint and stored response, request fingerprint to detect key reuse with a different body, in-flight vs completed states for concurrent retries, plus an outbox table written in the same local transaction and drained by a relay to the broker
gaps.why: Highest-value product-company gap, and the one his own notes set up without code: he has Payment_System_Design.md and Distributed_Transactions_Saga_QA.md but no implementation. Every payments, orders or checkout interview asks 'the client retried POST /payments after a timeout — how do you avoid charging twice?' and then 'you wrote to your DB and the Kafka publish failed — now what?' The outbox is the standard answer to the dual-write problem and it is one question deep from any Saga discussion he starts. The parts that need real code are the concurrent-retry race (second request arrives while the first is still in flight) and consumer-side dedupe, since at-least-once delivery means the relay will publish twice.

gaps.problem: LSM-tree storage engine: WAL, memtable, SSTable flush and compaction
gaps.technique: Append-only write-ahead log with fsync, sorted in-memory memtable, flush to immutable sorted segment files with a sparse index, merged read across segments newest-first, tombstones for deletes, size-tiered vs levelled compaction
gaps.why: His WideColumnStore is a nested HashMap with no durability and no ordering, so the moment he offers Cassandra or HBase in a design, the drill-down 'what actually happens on disk when I write' has nothing behind it. This is also the problem that explains, in one artifact, why these stores are write-optimised, why deletes are tombstones rather than removals, why reads get slower as segments accumulate, why compaction exists and what it costs in write amplification, and why the Bloom filter and sparse index are needed at all. It is the single highest-leverage addition for connecting his storage answers, and it subsumes the crash-recovery question ('the node died between the memtable write and the flush') that he currently cannot answer with code.

gaps.problem: Quorum-replicated key-value store with N/R/W, read repair and hinted handoff
gaps.technique: Configurable N replicas with R and W thresholds, R+W>N for overlap, coordinator scatter-gather with timeouts, read repair on stale replica detection, hinted handoff buffering writes for a down node
gaps.why: His notes cover quorum consensus in prose but no code exercises it, and this is the piece that ties his three existing storage problems into one story: the ring picks the N replicas, quorum decides when a write is acknowledged, Merkle trees repair what quorum missed. The interview ask is usually phrased as tunable consistency: 'what does R=1, W=1 give you versus R=2, W=2 on N=3, and when would you deliberately choose the weaker one?' A small simulator with injectable node failures is what makes the answer concrete, and it is where sloppy reasoning shows up, because R+W>N guarantees overlap but still does not give you linearizability without read repair or a real consensus protocol.

gaps.problem: Distributed lock and leader election with leases and fencing tokens
gaps.technique: Lease-based lock with TTL and owner token, heartbeat renewal, safe release via compare-and-delete on owner id, monotonically increasing fencing token checked by the resource, and the failure case where a paused holder's lease expires
gaps.why: The standard answer to a family of questions every backend loop asks: 'this cron job runs on 6 instances, how do you make only one execute', 'two workers grabbed the same queue item', 'who is the primary after the old one stops responding'. His notes mention strong consistency via distributed locking but there is no code, and the part that separates a senior answer from a staff answer is the fencing token: a GC pause or network partition can leave an old holder believing it still owns the lock, so the lock alone is unsafe and the protected resource must reject writes carrying a stale token. That argument is hard to make convincingly without having written the token check.
